newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: EU strikes price deal, delays grain aid cuts.
newsitem.headline: EU strikes price deal, delays grain aid cuts.

text.p: European Union farm ministers agreed on Wednesday, the third day of marathon price fixing talks, a package of measures for the coming year and delayed a proposed cut in aid to wealthy wheat farmers.

Agreement was reached on a third compromise brokered by Dutch Farm Minister Jozias Van Aartsen which satisfied some of the long wish list of sweeteners sought by ministers to satisfy impatient farmers back home.

EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler, who found support only from Britain and Sweden for 1.4 billion ecus ($1.6 billion) of cereals cuts intended to provide aid for beef producers devastated by the mad cow crisis, went down fighting.
"Failure to accept the proposal to reduce arable aid could have implications for many farming sectors in 1998," he warned after the meeting.

"There are strict budget restrictions in 1998," Van Aartsen told a closing news conference, adding these should not obstruct upcoming reform negotiations to prepare for the EU's expansion eastwards and the next round of world trade talks.
France's new farm minister Louis Le Pensec welcomed the deal, saying French demands on cereals set-aside, beef and other items had been met. "The compromise meets all French demands."
Set-aside is a scheme intended to remove costly grain mountains, under which farmers must take a certain percentage of their land out of production to obtain EU subsidies.
German Farm Minister Jochen Borchert noted that the deal meant German cereals farmers would avoid cuts totalling 630 million marks.
British Farm Minister Jack Cunningham welcomed the agreement, saying that it included a commitment to start a review of the cereals, beef and dairy sectors.
"It will be a major item during the British EU Presidency (January-June 1998)," he told reporters.
Britain also won a commitment for the Commission to examine special health and welfare measures for the transport of breeding pigs -- an export trade worth 90 million pounds a year.
Only Spain was unhappy with the deal which failed to meet its wishes on milk quotas, olive oil, wine and other products.
Key points in the Dutch compromise were calls for the cereals set-aside rate to be maintained at five percent in 1998 and a suspension of penalties on farmers who overplanted for another two years.
But the EU's embattled Austrian farm chief, Franz Fischler, said it was too early to fix the 1998 set-aside rate and added that he did not have to follow the wishes of farm ministers.
"The Commission is free to make a proposal and that's what we'll do as soon as possible," Fischler told journalists.
He does not want to be bounced into a hasty proposal until he has all the necessary crop and weather data.
Regarding cereals subsidies, Fischler insisted on a 7.3 percent cut in payments, which mainly benefit wealthy grain producers in Britain, France and Germany.

The Commission estimated that grain farmers, who already receive the lion's share of EU farm subsidies, were overpaid by 8.5 billion ecus during the past four years for cuts in support prices agreed under 1992 farm reforms.
Farmers were still paid even though market prices soared after bad weather hit crops across the world and grain stocks slumped to the lowest levels for 20 years.

An overwhelming majority of farm ministers disagreed that grain farmers were overpaid. They said it was unfair to make them foot the bill and that there was enough spare cash in the 1997 budget to aid beef producers.
